title: Swift tutorial: optionals, structs, enums and protocols — cv.cm
description: Learn Swift in one page: Hello world, let and var, types, control flow, closures, arrays and dictionaries, optionals, structs, enums and errors.
answer: Swift is a fast, safe, compiled language created by Apple for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch and Apple TV apps, and it also runs on Linux and Windows. Save `print("Hello, world")` in `hello.swift` and run `swift hello.swift`. The core ideas are `let` constants and `var` variables, type inference, optionals for values that may be missing, structs and enums with value semantics, protocols, and errors handled with `do`/`try`/`catch`.

sections.h: What Swift is and what it is used for
body: Swift was introduced by Apple in 2014 as a modern replacement for Objective-C and was open-sourced in 2015; the project lives at swift.org. It is the main language for apps on Apple platforms, usually with the SwiftUI or UIKit frameworks. Swift is also used for server-side code (for example with the Vapor framework) and command-line tools. The language is designed to prevent common bugs: variables must be initialized, arrays check their bounds, and `nil` must be handled explicitly.

sections.h: Install Swift and run Hello, world
body: On a Mac, install Xcode from the App Store or the Xcode command-line tools. On Linux and Windows, download a toolchain from swift.org. Check it with `swift --version`.

body.code:
swift hello.swift
# Hello, world
swiftc hello.swift -o hello   # compile to a binary
./hello

body: For a larger project, run `swift package init --type executable` and then `swift run`. Xcode playgrounds are another easy way to experiment.
Use `let` for constants and `var` for variables. Prefer `let`; the compiler warns when a `var` is never changed. Types are inferred, and Swift never converts between numeric types implicitly.

body.code:
let name = "Ada"
var count = 7
count += 1
let avg = Double(count) / 2   // explicit conversion
print("\(name) has \(count) items, avg \(avg)")  // Ada has 8 items, avg 4.0
print(7 / 2, 7 % 2)          // 3 1

body: `\(expression)` inside a string literal inserts a value (string interpolation).
`switch` must be exhaustive, does not fall through by default, and can match ranges (`case 90...100:`), tuples and enum cases.
Parameters have argument labels that callers write, which makes calls read like sentences. Use `_` to omit a label. Closures are unnamed functions written in braces.
`$0` refers to the first closure argument. When a closure is the last argument, it can be written after the parentheses (trailing closure syntax).

body.code:
var fruits = ["apple", "pear"]
fruits.append("fig")
print(fruits.count, fruits[0], fruits.contains("fig"))  // 3 apple true

var ages: [String: Int] = ["ann": 31, "bob": 25]
ages["cy"] = 40
for (person, age) in ages.sorted(by: { $0.key < $1.key }) {
    print(person, age)                                  // ann 31, bob 25, cy 40
}
print(ages["zed", default: 0])                          // 0

let tags: Set = ["b", "a", "b"]
print(tags.count)                                       // 2

body: Collections are value types: assigning an array to another variable creates an independent copy (copied lazily, only when one of them changes). A `let` array cannot be modified at all.
A value that may be missing has an optional type, written `String?`. You cannot use it as a `String` until you unwrap it, so the compiler forces you to handle the `nil` case.

`if let` and `guard let` unwrap safely, `?.` (optional chaining) calls a method only when the value exists, and `??` supplies a default. The force unwrap `value!` crashes when the value is `nil`, so use it rarely. The short form `if let number` needs Swift 5.7 or later.
Structs and enums are value types; classes are reference types with inheritance. Swift code favors structs and protocols (interfaces) over class hierarchies.
Structs get a memberwise initializer automatically (`Rect(width:height:)`). Enum cases can carry associated values, as `.radius(Double)` does.
Functions that can fail are marked `throws`. Callers must use `try` inside a `do`/`catch` block, or use `try?` to turn an error into `nil`.

sections.h: A small complete program: word frequency
body: Run it with `swift words.swift notes.txt`. `Foundation` provides file reading and string helpers; it is available on Apple platforms and in the Linux and Windows toolchains.

body.note: Avoid force unwrapping with `!` and implicitly unwrapped types such as `String!` except where a value is guaranteed. A `nil` at that point crashes the app at runtime.

ul: Trying to change a `let` constant or a property of a `let` struct. Use `var` when the value must change.
Expecting a struct to be shared like an object. Changing a copy does not change the original; use a class if you need shared identity.
Indexing a `String` with an integer, such as `s[0]`. Use `s.first`, `s.prefix(3)` or `String.Index` values.
Mixing `Int` and `Double` in arithmetic without converting, which is a compile error.
Forgetting `try` before a throwing call, or using `try!`, which crashes on error.

body: Read "The Swift Programming Language" on docs.swift.org, the official guide and reference, and the documentation hub on swift.org. For apps, follow Apple's SwiftUI tutorials in Xcode. Then learn Swift concurrency (`async`/`await` and actors), generics, and the Swift Package Manager for dependencies.

faq.q: Is Swift only for Apple platforms?
faq.a: No. Swift is open source and runs on Linux and Windows too, and it is used for server-side code and tools. However, app frameworks such as SwiftUI and UIKit are Apple-only.

faq.q: Should I learn Swift or Objective-C?
faq.a: Learn Swift. It is Apple's recommended language for new apps, and it can call existing Objective-C code when needed.

faq.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class in Swift?
faq.a: A struct is a value type that is copied when assigned or passed; a class is a reference type, so all variables share one instance. Classes also support inheritance and deinitializers.

faq.q: What does the question mark after a type mean?
faq.a: `Int?` is an optional: it holds either an `Int` or `nil`. You must unwrap it, for example with `if let`, before using the value.
